title: Packages, Modules & go.mod
summary: Go organizes code into **packages** (a folder of related .go files) and groups packages into a **module** described by a `go.mod` file. The module is your unit of versioning and dependency management; `go.mod` records the module path, the Go version, and every dependency with its exact version.

subtopics.title: What a package is
subtopics.explanation: A package is all the .go files in a single directory that share the same `package` name. Code in the same package can see each other's identifiers directly; package main is special — it builds an executable.
subtopics.example: package store // every file in ./store starts with this

subtopics.title: Exported vs unexported (capitalization)
subtopics.explanation: An identifier is exported (visible to other packages) if it starts with a capital letter, and unexported (package-private) if it starts lowercase. There's no `public`/`private` keyword — capitalization IS the access control.
subtopics.example:
func Save() {}   // exported
func parse() {}  // unexported

subtopics.title: What a module is
subtopics.explanation: A module is a collection of packages versioned together, identified by a module path (usually a repo URL) and described by go.mod at its root. It is the unit you publish, depend on, and version.
subtopics.example: module github.com/me/store // first line of go.mod

subtopics.title: go.mod and go.sum
subtopics.explanation: go.mod lists the module path, the Go version, and required dependencies with versions. go.sum records cryptographic checksums of those dependencies so builds are verifiable and tamper-resistant. Commit both.

subtopics.title: import paths
subtopics.explanation: You import a package by its full path: the module path plus the directory inside it. The last path element is usually (but not always) the package name you reference in code.

subtopics.title: go get & go mod tidy
subtopics.explanation: `go get pkg@version` adds or upgrades a dependency; `go mod tidy` syncs go.mod/go.sum to exactly what your code imports — adding missing requirements and removing unused ones. Run tidy before committing.
subtopics.example:
go get github.com/google/uuid@v1.6.0
go mod tidy

foundations.overview: Go code doesn't live in a single file — it's grouped into packages, and packages are grouped into a module. A package is just a directory of .go files that declare the same package name and can freely use each other's functions and types. A module wraps one or more packages under a single name (its module path) and is described by a go.mod file at the module root. go.mod is the heart of dependency management: it names your module, pins the Go version, and lists exactly which external packages and versions you depend on. This system makes Go builds reproducible and dependencies explicit.
foundations.formalDefinition: A package is the unit of compilation and namespacing in Go — the set of source files in one directory sharing a package clause. A module is a versioned collection of packages with a go.mod file at its root declaring the module path and dependency requirements; it is the unit of dependency management and distribution.
foundations.whyItMatters: Every Go project is a module, and every line of code lives in a package. Knowing how imports resolve, how go.mod pins versions, and how capitalization controls visibility is essential to structuring real projects and is frequently probed in interviews.
foundations.mentalModel: Think of a module as a library building (go.mod is the directory listing at the entrance), packages as the rooms (each holds related books/code), and exported names as the books on the public shelves while unexported names are kept in the staff-only back office.
foundations.runtimePerspective: Packages are a compile-time concept: the compiler resolves imports, compiles each package once, and links them. go.mod tells the toolchain where to fetch dependencies and which exact versions to use, downloading them into the module cache so builds are reproducible.
foundations.realWorldUsage: Splitting a service into packages (handlers, store, models), publishing reusable libraries as modules, and pinning third-party dependencies (logging, UUIDs, database drivers) via go.mod.
foundations.businessImpact: Reproducible, checksum-verified dependencies (go.sum) reduce supply-chain risk and 'works on my machine' failures, protecting release reliability.
foundations.engineeringImpact: Clear package boundaries and capitalization-based visibility enforce encapsulation, making large codebases maintainable; explicit go.mod versions make upgrades deliberate.
foundations.performanceImpact: Packages compile independently and are cached, so changing one package only rebuilds it and its dependents — keeping incremental builds fast in large modules.
commonUseCases: Splitting a service into cohesive packages
Declaring a module with `go mod init`
Keeping go.mod/go.sum clean with go mod tidy

commonMisconceptions.myth: The package name must match the directory name.
commonMisconceptions.reality: It usually does by convention, but the package clause is what matters; the import path is the directory, the referenced name is the package clause.
They pin exact versions; combined with go.sum checksums, builds are reproducible and verified against tampering.
Visibility is decided by the first letter's case: uppercase is exported, lowercase is package-private.

config.intro: What happens when you import a package in a module:

steps.name: Read go.mod
steps.detail: The toolchain reads the module path and required dependency versions from go.mod at the module root.

steps.name: Match the import path
steps.detail: The import path is the module path plus a subdirectory; the toolchain locates that package inside your module or a dependency.

steps.name: Fetch if external
steps.detail: External dependencies are downloaded at the pinned version into the module cache and verified against go.sum checksums.

steps.name: Compile the package
steps.detail: Each package is compiled once; only exported (capitalized) identifiers are accessible to importers.

steps.name: Link
steps.detail: Compiled packages are linked into the final binary. go mod tidy keeps go.mod aligned with what's actually imported.

interactiveExamples.title: A package with exported and unexported names
interactiveExamples.explanation: In package mathx, Add is exported (capital A) so other packages can call it; the helper is unexported. main imports mathx by its path and calls only the exported function.

interactiveExamples.title: Edit it: export the function
interactiveExamples.explanation: main can't see `area` because it's unexported. Rename it so it starts with a capital letter and update the call. This shows how capitalization is Go's access control.

checkpoints.prompt: Which identifier is accessible from another package?
checkpoints.explanation: Exported identifiers start with an uppercase letter: Save and Count are visible to other packages; load and total are lowercase and therefore package-private.

checkpoints.prompt: Create a new module named github.com/me/app.
checkpoints.codeAfter: # creates go.mod with that module path
checkpoints.explanation: go mod init <path> creates a go.mod file declaring the module path. go get adds dependencies; there is no plain `go init`.

checkpoints.prompt: go.mod lists a dependency the code no longer imports, and the build still works. What command cleans this up?
options: go mod tidy syncs go.mod/go.sum to actual imports
checkpoints.explanation: go mod tidy adds any missing requirements and removes ones no longer imported, keeping go.mod and go.sum aligned with the code. Build won't prune unused requires on its own.

checkpoints.prompt: Given import path "github.com/me/store/cart", which name do you use in code (typical case)?
checkpoints.explanation: You reference a package by its package name — usually the last path element. Here that's cart, so you call cart.New(). The full path is only used in the import statement.

codeLab.title: Design a tiny package API
codeLab.instructions: In package solution, implement an exported `Normalize(s string) string` that trims surrounding spaces and lowercases the input, using an unexported helper `clean` internally. The point: expose only what callers need.
hints: strings.TrimSpace removes leading/trailing whitespace; strings.ToLower lowercases.
Keep the helper lowercase (unexported) so it stays internal.
Only Normalize should be exported — that's your package's public surface.

debuggingLab.title: Cannot find package
debuggingLab.symptom: Build fails: no required module provides package github.com/google/uuid; to add it: go get github.com/google/uuid.
debuggingLab.errorAnalysis: You imported an external package, but go.mod has no requirement for it and it isn't in the module cache. Go won't guess versions silently — you must add the dependency so the version is pinned and recorded in go.mod/go.sum.
commonMistakes: Importing a third-party package without running go get.
Editing import statements but forgetting to run go mod tidy.
debuggingLab.fixChallenge: Add the dependency and sync go.mod/go.sum.

theory.question: What is the difference between a package and a module in Go?
theory.directAnswer: A package is a single directory of .go files sharing a package name — the unit of compilation and namespacing. A module is a versioned collection of packages with a go.mod file at its root, identified by a module path; it's the unit of dependency management and distribution. A module contains one or more packages.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Package = one directory's code; module = a versioned group of packages described by go.mod.
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: Packages give namespacing and encapsulation; modules give versioning and reproducible dependencies.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: Imports resolve to packages by path; go.mod pins the versions of external modules those packages come from.

theory.whyImportant: Confusing the two leads to broken imports and dependency mistakes; it's a foundational interview question.
theory.realWorldExample: A service module github.com/acme/api contains packages handlers, store, and models.

followUps.question: Can one repo have multiple modules?
followUps.answer: Yes, but it's uncommon; usually one go.mod per repo at the root.

followUps.question: What does package main mean?
followUps.answer: It marks an executable program with a main() entry point, as opposed to a library package.

theory.question: How does Go control what is visible across packages?
theory.directAnswer: By the case of the first letter of an identifier. Uppercase means exported (visible to importing packages); lowercase means unexported (visible only within the declaring package). There are no public/private keywords — capitalization is the access control.

detailedExplanation.whatItIs: Capitalization-based export rules for names (functions, types, variables, fields).
detailedExplanation.whyItExists: A simple, uniform rule for encapsulation without extra keywords.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: The compiler rejects references to lowercase identifiers from other packages.

theory.whyImportant: Designing a clean package API hinges on choosing what to export; this comes up constantly.
theory.realWorldExample: A store package exports New() and Get() but keeps connection-pool internals lowercase.

followUps.question: Does this apply to struct fields too?
followUps.answer: Yes — only capitalized struct fields are visible outside the package (and to encoders like encoding/json).

scenario.question: A build works on your machine but fails for a teammate with a checksum mismatch on a dependency. What's likely wrong and how do you keep builds reproducible?
scenario.directAnswer: go.sum was probably not committed or got out of sync, so the teammate's downloaded dependency didn't match the recorded checksum. Commit both go.mod and go.sum, run go mod tidy to align them with the code, and ensure everyone uses the same pinned versions. go.sum makes dependency contents verifiable across machines.

detailedExplanation.whyItExists: go.sum stores cryptographic checksums so the exact same bytes are used everywhere.
detailedExplanation.howItWorks: On download, Go verifies the dependency against go.sum and fails if it differs.

scenario.whyImportant: Reproducible, verified builds prevent supply-chain attacks and 'works on my machine' bugs.
scenario.realWorldExample: CI fails fast on a tampered or mismatched dependency because go.sum verification fails.

followUps.question: Should go.sum be committed?
followUps.answer: Yes — both go.mod and go.sum belong in version control.

coding.question: Design a small package `validate` with an exported func IsEmail(s string) bool that uses an unexported helper. Show the package code.
coding.thoughtProcess: Expose only the high-level check; hide the regex/parsing detail in an unexported helper. A minimal check: contains exactly one @ with non-empty local and domain parts.
coding.lineByLine: IsEmail delegates to hasSingleAt, keeping the public surface tiny. hasSingleAt finds the @ index; if it's missing, first, or last, the address is invalid. It then ensures there's exactly one @. Only IsEmail is exported, so callers can't depend on the helper.

followUps.question: Why keep hasSingleAt unexported?
followUps.answer: It's an implementation detail; hiding it lets you change validation later without breaking callers.

productionDeepDive.architecture: Structure a service into cohesive packages with clear public APIs (export the minimum). Keep go.mod at the repo root and avoid import cycles, which Go forbids and which usually signal a layering problem.
productionDeepDive.performance: Per-package compilation and caching keep large modules building fast; minimizing exported surface reduces coupling and rebuild fan-out.
productionDeepDive.concurrency: Package boundaries help isolate shared state; keep concurrency primitives encapsulated behind a package's exported API so callers can't misuse internals.
productionDeepDive.reliability: Commit go.mod and go.sum, pin dependency versions, and run go mod tidy in CI to catch drift. go.sum verification protects against tampered dependencies.
productionDeepDive.observability: Use go list -m all to audit the full dependency tree and go mod why to explain why a dependency is present, aiding security reviews.
productionDeepDive.security: go.sum + the Go checksum database verify dependency integrity; vendor or proxy dependencies (GOPROXY) for supply-chain control and reproducibility.

caseStudies.problem: Keeping dependencies consistent across many services.
caseStudies.solution: Single module per service with committed go.mod/go.sum and CI running go mod tidy.
caseStudies.tradeoffs: Discipline required, but builds stay reproducible.
caseStudies.lessons: Explicit, pinned, verified dependencies are essential at scale.

caseStudies.problem: Avoiding breaking downstream users on upgrades.
caseStudies.solution: Careful export decisions and semantic-version module paths (e.g. /v2).
caseStudies.lessons: What you export becomes a contract; export the minimum.

keyTakeaways: A package is a directory of .go files sharing a package name; a module is a versioned group of packages described by go.mod.
Capitalization controls visibility: uppercase identifiers are exported, lowercase are package-private.
go.mod pins the module path, Go version, and dependency versions; go.sum records checksums for reproducible, verified builds — commit both.
Use go mod init to start a module, go get to add dependencies, and go mod tidy to keep go.mod/go.sum in sync with your imports.
